interactions.student_prompt_or_question: Explain the problem setting of Force-Directed List-Scheduling for High-Level Synthesis in simple terms.
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Clarified that HLS scheduling maps operations from a behavioral/data-flow description to clock/control steps while respecting dependencies and resource limits. FDLS was framed as a heuristic that combines list scheduling with force-based priority estimation.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will draw a small data-flow graph with add/multiply nodes and show why several valid schedules can produce different hardware costs.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: The explanation will be rewritten in my own words; I will cite HLS scheduling background and the FDLS source when mentioning the algorithm.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: Identify the motivation: why is scheduling necessary in HLS before RTL generation?
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Explained that scheduling determines when operations execute, which affects latency, number of functional units, registers, buses, and therefore area/performance tradeoffs.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will connect this with the professor's requirement that the output of HLS is an RTL/netlist-level implementation.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: No copied wording will be used; the source will be cited for the HLS flow and synthesis tasks.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: List the core formal objects I need: problem graph, operations, dependencies, resources, time steps, latency bound, and resource constraint.
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Defined a scheduling problem with a directed acyclic problem graph, operation types, resource types, control steps, precedence constraints, mobility intervals, and either time-constrained or resource-constrained objectives.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will use a compact notation table in Milestone 1 and keep the equations short.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: Formal notation will be student-authored and citations will support the source concepts.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: Explain ASAP and ALAP because FDLS uses time frames and mobility.
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Summarized ASAP as earliest feasible scheduling under dependencies and ALAP as latest feasible scheduling under a latency bound. Their difference gives mobility/time frame information.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will compute ASAP/ALAP manually for a small example graph to prove understanding.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: The algorithm names are standard; any descriptive text will be written freshly and cited.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: Explain force-directed scheduling without copying the paper: what are probability, distribution graph, and force?
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Explained that unscheduled operations are spread over feasible time frames; their probabilities contribute to resource usage distribution. A force estimates how assigning an operation to one step changes resource pressure and successor/predecessor mobility.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will present this as intuition plus one simple formula rather than reproduce paper text.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: The terms are technical; all definitions will be paraphrased and cited.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: What is the difference between Force-Directed Scheduling and Force-Directed List-Scheduling?
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Clarified that classic FDS is often time-constrained and tries to reduce resource usage by balancing concurrency; FDLS adapts force as a priority in a list-scheduling style when resource constraints are fixed.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will explicitly state this distinction because my topic is FDLS, not only FDS.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: This distinction will be cited from the relevant Paulin and Knight work and checked in the original reference if accessible.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: Give an algorithm skeleton for FDLS that I can later implement in C++.
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Produced a high-level skeleton: build ready list, compute ASAP/ALAP/time frames, compute force-based priorities, choose ready operation/resource/control step, schedule it, update time frames and priorities, repeat until all nodes are scheduled.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will implement a simplified version for unit-delay operations and two resource types for the seminar example.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: The implementation will be original code and simplified assumptions will be clearly stated.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: What assumptions should I mention in Milestone 1?
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Identified assumptions: static/offline scheduling, known operation graph, known operation latencies, finite resource types, no dynamic branch behavior in the minimal example, and simplified binding/interconnect estimation unless extended.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will add an assumptions subsection and avoid claiming optimality.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: Assumptions are my own framing based on the cited HLS model.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: What runtime, memory, or scalability aspects should be discussed at first-milestone level?
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Explained that exact ILP can be optimal but may scale poorly, while FDLS is heuristic and repeatedly recomputes priorities/time-frame effects. Memory mainly stores graph, ready list, time frames, probabilities, and distribution arrays.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will describe complexity qualitatively in Milestone 1 and later make it more critical in Milestone 3.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: I will avoid unsupported Big-O claims unless I can justify them from algorithm structure or a cited source.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: What should be my unclear points/questions for feedback?
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Suggested questions: how detailed should the C++ implementation be, whether to include binding/interconnect costs, whether to compare against ILP or simple list scheduling, and what size of example is acceptable for a 5-page IEEE paper.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will include 4-5 feedback questions at the end of the briefing.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: These are my own feedback questions, not claims from sources.

interactions.student_prompt_or_question: Create a Milestone 1 outline matching the professor's expected output.
interactions.ai_assistance_summary: Created a structured 2-4 page outline: problem/motivation, core idea, formal model, algorithm sketch, assumptions/scope, resource aspects, unclear points.
interactions.student_verification_or_next_action: I will fill this outline myself using my example and citations.
interactions.academic_integrity_note: The outline is allowed as planning support; final prose must be authored by me.

plagiarism_prevention: No source text is copied into the generated interaction logs.
Every technical claim intended for later use is linked to a reference key.
Final report and slides must be written in the student's own words.
Bibliographic details must be verified in Zotero/Citavi before submission.
AI outputs are treated as planning, explanation, and checking support, not as final authored prose.
academic_integrity_policy.citation_rule_for_later_work: Cite sources near the relevant technical claim: HLS/scheduling background, FDLS/FDS origin, comparison with ILP/list scheduling, and course-specific requirements.
